name: Relighting and Shading
text:
# Relighting and Shading


## Overview
Relighting and Shading techniques address the problem of lighting inconsistency when [compositing](#2436-compositing.md) objects into [neural radiance field (NeRF)](#834-neural-radiance-field-nerf.md) scenes or synthesizing novel views under varying illumination conditions [G]. Unlike standard radiance field methods that treat radiance as a static view-dependent signal, this family explicitly models lighting interactions, inter-reflections, or shading correlations to enable physically plausible relighting and HDR synthesis [G]. It sets itself apart from direct relighting methods by either replacing object shading based on scene correlations [Shading Replacement for Relighting](6346-shading-replacement-for-relighting.md) or integrating [surface rendering](#22224-surface-rendering.md) principles into the volume rendering framework to model irradiance [Pano-NeRF](15013-pano-nerf.md).

## Shared principles
The core mechanism involves decoupling or explicitly modeling the illumination component of the radiance field [G]. In [standard NeRF](#979-nerf-volumetric-rendering-coarse-fine-sampling.md), radiance $c(x, \mathbf{d})$ is a direct output of the network [G]. In this family, the representation is extended to account for how light interacts with geometry [G].

1. **Irradiance-Radiance Coupling**: Radiance is treated as both a signal conveying lighting information and a light source illuminating other pixels [Pano-NeRF](15013-pano-nerf.md). This increases observation counts for geometry and leverages irradiance-radiance attenuation for High Dynamic Range (HDR) reconstruction [Pano-NeRF](15013-pano-nerf.md).
2. **Surface-Volume Integration**: Methods may integrate surface rendering principles ([BRDF](#14809-bidirectional-reflectance-distribution-function-brdf.md), normals) into the volumetric framework [Pano-NeRF](15013-pano-nerf.md). For instance, outgoing radiance $C_i(x)$ is computed by integrating irradiance from incoming light directions $\omega_i$ over a sphere $\Omega$ centered at $x$ [Pano-NeRF](15013-pano-nerf.md):
$$ C_i(x) = \int_{\omega_i \in \Omega} f_r(x, \omega_o, \omega_i) \cdot \max(\omega_i \cdot \mathbf{n}, 0) \cdot c_i(x, \omega_i) \, d\omega_i $$
where $f_r$ is the BRDF, $\mathbf{n}$ is the surface normal, and $c_i(x, \omega_i)$ is the incoming radiance computed via volume rendering [Pano-NeRF](15013-pano-nerf.md).
3. **Shading Correlation**: In object insertion tasks, shading is inferred by correlating surface [normals and shading](#1831-normal-shading.md) values between the inserted object and the existing scene, avoiding explicit light source estimation [Shading Replacement for Relighting](6346-shading-replacement-for-relighting.md).

## Subtopics

### [Shading Replacement for Relighting](6346-shading-replacement-for-relighting.md)
[Shading Replacement for Relighting](#6346-shading-replacement-for-relighting.md) is a technique for object insertion that avoids inferring scene illumination by replacing the inserted object's shading with shading from existing scene points [Shading Replacement for Relighting](6346-shading-replacement-for-relighting.md). It solves the problem of lighting inconsistency when compositing objects into [NeRF](#1185-nerf-neural-radiance-fields.md) scenes, where naive composition leads to unrealistic results due to varying illumination [Shading Replacement for Relighting](6346-shading-replacement-for-relighting.md). It sets itself apart from direct relighting methods by not requiring explicit light source estimation, instead relying on the correlation between surface normals and shading in Lambertian scenes [Shading Replacement for Relighting](6346-shading-replacement-for-relighting.md). Choose this method when inserting objects into a scene where the lighting environment is complex and unknown, but surface normals are available or estimable.

### [Pano-NeRF](15013-pano-nerf.md)
[Pano-NeRF](#15013-pano-nerf.md) is a method for geometry recovery and High Dynamic Range (HDR) novel view synthesis from sparse Low Dynamic Range (LDR) panoramic images [Pano-NeRF](15013-pano-nerf.md). It models the scene using irradiance fields, which treat radiance as both a signal conveying lighting information and a light source illuminating other pixels, thereby increasing observation counts for geometry and leveraging irradiance-radiance attenuation for HDR reconstruction [Pano-NeRF](15013-pano-nerf.md). It differs from standard radiance field methods by integrating surface rendering principles into the volume rendering framework to explicitly model inter-reflection and lighting interactions [Pano-NeRF](15013-pano-nerf.md). Choose this method when working with sparse panoramic inputs and requiring HDR output or improved geometry recovery through [inter-reflection modeling](#15367-inter-reflection-modeling.md).

### [IllumiNeRF](18157-illuminerf.md)
[IllumiNeRF](#18157-illuminerf.md) is a 3D [relighting pipeline](#18921-multi-light-rendering-relighting-integration.md) that reconstructs a relightable 3D representation from posed input images under unknown lighting by generating multiple plausible relit images via a diffusion model and distilling them into a consistent 3D [latent NeRF](#9110-latent-nerf.md), avoiding inverse rendering [IllumiNeRF](18157-illuminerf.md). Unlike inverse rendering which recovers a single point estimate of geometry and materials, IllumiNeRF samples multiple plausible explanations of materials, geometry, and lighting, reconciling them into a single 3D representation that can be rendered from novel viewpoints under a target environment illumination [IllumiNeRF](18157-illuminerf.md). Choose this method when handling lighting ambiguity and requiring consistent relighting without explicit [inverse rendering optimization](#8999-inverse-rendering-and-optimization.md).

### [Neural Reflectance Fields](22620-neural-reflectance-fields.md)
[Neural Reflectance Fields](#22620-neural-reflectance-fields.md) is the first extension of [Neural Radiance Fields](#4972-neural-radiance-fields.md) (NeRF) to enable relighting by representing a scene as a field of volume density, surface normals, and bi-directional reflectance distribution functions (BRDFs) rather than just density and emitted radiance. It solves the problem of view-dependent appearance under unknown or arbitrary lighting by decoupling material properties from illumination. Unlike standard NeRF, which models radiance as a direct function of position and view direction, Neural Reflectance Fields models the physical [interaction](#41-interaction.md) of light with volume particles, allowing the scene to be rendered under new lighting conditions. It differs from siblings like [Pano-NeRF](15013-pano-nerf.md) and [IllumiNeRF](18157-illuminerf.md) by explicitly predicting BRDF parameters and normals per voxel to compute reflected radiance, whereas other methods may rely on spherical Gaussian mixtures or assume full visibility. Choose this method when explicit per-voxel material and normal prediction is required for novel lighting synthesis.

### CI-NeRF
CI-NeRF utilizes NeRF for volumetric rendering to deduce essential scene characteristics like diffuse albedo, surface normals, shadows, and lighting settings [S1]. It employs a [CNN](#20776-2d-convolutional-neural-network-cnn.md) for forecasting interpretable and modifiable lighting parameters from an individual image [S1]. This allows for the physical interpretation of outdoor scene relighting through a unified image inference process, enhancing both the quality and realism of the relighting [S1].

### Indirect Illumination via Radiance Field Derivation
Indirect Illumination via Radiance Field Derivation is an approach to efficiently recover spatially-varying indirect illumination in inverse rendering by deriving it from a learned neural radiance field, avoiding expensive recursive path tracing [S2]. It learns the geometry and outgoing radiance field of the object, both represented as MLPs, from input images using an existing method (e.g., [IDR](#20341-idr-implicit-differentiable-renderer.md) [27]) [S2]. It uses the learned radiance field as ground-truth incoming illumination for reachable surface points to train a separate indirect illumination MLP [S2]. It plugs the learned indirect illumination into the rendering equation and fixes it during the optimization of SVBRDF and environmental light [S2]. It queries the indirect illumination directly when optimizing other unknowns, eliminating the need for recursive path tracing [S2].

### NeRV
[NeRV](#10246-nerv-neural-reflectance-and-visibility-fields.md) uses a second "visibility" MLP to support arbitrary [environment lighting](#17399-environment-map-as-image-based-lighting.md) and "one-bounce" indirect illumination [S3, unofficial].

## Background
The concept of integrating lighting and shading into neural radiance fields has evolved to address limitations in standard NeRF regarding physical plausibility and dynamic lighting [G]. CI-NeRF (2023) was introduced to allow physical interpretation of outdoor scene relighting through a unified image inference process, surpassing current methods in inherent image breakdown and real-world landmark scene relighting [S1]. Pano-NeRF and Shading Replacement for Relighting further extend this by explicitly handling irradiance fields and shading correlations, respectively, to solve issues in sparse view synthesis and object compositing [Pano-NeRF](15013-pano-nerf.md, 6346-shading-replacement-for-relighting.md). These methods build on the foundational NeRF architecture but modify the query and rendering process to include lighting-aware representations [G].

## Sources

[S2] Modeling Indirect Illumination for Inverse Rendering, https://doi.org/10.1109/cvpr52688.2022.01809, fetched 2026-10-26
